title: Bacteria sense virus-induced genome degradation via methylated mononucleotides.

verified.what_i_actually_checked: Europe PMC record (not open access, hasSuppl=N, hasData=N, no database cross-references); NCBI links (the only PMC hit, PMC12871103, is a different paper by another group); Europe PMC accession text-mining (only two Pfam protein-family IDs, PF00149 and PF13419 - no sequence or dataset accessions); Europe PMC supplementaryFiles endpoint for the open preprint PPR1114940 (returned an empty 'JsonNull' error); Zenodo search on the DOI and title (no deposit); NCBI BioProject searches for the system name and the senior author (0 hits); Science landing page (HTTP 403, subscription); bioRxiv supplementary ZIP at two URL patterns, with and without browser headers (HTTP 429 every time, ~6 attempts). I did read the open preprint's full text, which lists exactly one supplementary ZIP containing Tables S1-S4.
verified.what_came_from_paper_text_only: All content facts: Table S1 = homologs of MisB (the sensor protein) drawn from 38,167 bacterial and archaeal genomes in IMG (Integrated Microbial Genomes); Table S2 = PCR primers; Table S3 = plasmids, strains and phages; Table S4 = isolated phage escaper mutants. Experiments: roughly 3-4 defense systems cloned into E. coli and challenged with 5 lytic phages (T2, T4, T5, T6, T7), plaque assays and LC-MS (liquid chromatography-mass spectrometry) metabolomics in triplicate. No count of total Metis systems is given anywhere in the text, and there is no data-availability or code-availability statement.

a1_downloadable.note: No deposited dataset exists anywhere: no GEO, SRA, BioProject, Zenodo or Dryad entry, and Europe PMC flags hasData=N. The only data are supplementary tables behind the subscription Science site (HTTP 403) or inside one bioRxiv ZIP that returned HTTP 429 to every programmatic request. I could not open a single data file.

a2_label_is_a_column.note: Not verified in files, but clear from the text: there is no outcome column. Any machine-learning label ('does this protein family defend against phage?') would have to be constructed by hand from figure panels and from the handful of systems the authors cloned.

a3_inputs_present.note: Paper text only: Table S1 is a homolog list from IMG, so protein identifiers are present and sequences are retrievable from public databases, but I never saw the table.

a4_units_stated.note: Unverifiable. The quantitative readouts (fold protection in plaque assays, ion counts in mass spectrometry) live in figures, not in a table with a units column, as far as the text shows.

a5_enough_rows.note: The measured phenotype covers roughly 3-4 cloned defense systems against 5 phages (about 20 combinations in triplicate) - two orders of magnitude under the ~400-row floor for classification. The one large table (MisB homologs from 38,167 genomes) carries no measured outcome.

a6_fits_laptop.note: Size was never the problem; a few spreadsheets would fit easily.

a7_counts_match_paper.note: Cannot be checked: the paper states no homolog count to compare against, and I could not open the table.

a8_label_provenance.note: Where a phenotype exists it is a genuine wet-lab measurement (plaque assays, mass spectrometry), not another model's output - but it exists for only a few systems.

existing_models.name: DefensePredictor (Science 2026, doi 10.1126/science.adv7924) - classifies bacterial proteins as anti-phage defensive from protein language model embeddings
existing_models.score_and_split: Not verified - the article page was CAPTCHA-blocked. From search summaries: applied to 69 diverse Escherichia coli strains, predicted hundreds of unknown systems and experimentally validated 42; described as open-source software runnable on any prokaryotic genome.
existing_models.authors_named_unsolved: Per search summaries, 15 protein domains among the 42 validated systems had never been shown to be defensive, which the authors read as evidence that many immune mechanisms remain undiscovered.

existing_models.name: Protein and genomic language model pair of Mordret et al. (bioRxiv 2025.01.08.631966) - a fine-tuned ESM-2 protein language model plus an ALBERT-architecture genomic-context model for antiphage defense prediction
existing_models.score_and_split: Not verified - abstract-level only. Reported scanning over 120 million bacterial proteins and predicting hundreds of thousands of candidate antiphage families, with six systems validated experimentally in Actinomycetota.
existing_models.authors_named_unsolved: Abstract frames the uncharacterized defense repertoire (tens of thousands of predicted families) as the open problem; I did not read the discussion.

backbone.name: ESM-2 (protein language model, small CPU-runnable checkpoints)
backbone.hardware: Laptop CPU would suffice for embeddings, but there are almost no labelled examples to fit a head on.
backbone.licence: ESM-2 is MIT-licensed; the paper's preprint is CC-BY-NC-ND, which restricts reuse of its tables to non-commercial work.

integration.partner_dataset: UniProt / AlphaFold DB via the Pfam families named in the text (PF00149, PF13419), or DefenseFinder's curated system catalogue
integration.bigger_question_one_sentence: Which protein families across all sequenced bacteria sense degraded host DNA as an infection signal - a question this paper's few tested systems cannot answer, and which DefensePredictor-style models already attack with far more labels.

controls.positive_control: Known anti-phage systems in the same genomes (restriction-modification, CBASS) should score as defensive in any classifier - available, but only useful if labels existed.
controls.negative_control: Label shuffling is runnable in principle; with ~20 phenotype measurements it would be uninformative.
controls.external_validation: DefenseFinder / PADLOC catalogues of validated systems would serve as an independent label source, but that makes the other papers' datasets the project, not this one.

honest_claim_h3: With this paper alone a model could only claim 'among the three or four Metis systems these authors chose to clone, protection against five laboratory coliphages behaves as follows' - a statement about a handful of experiments, not a generalizable prediction.

plain_idea.one_liner: Use bacterial protein sequences to predict which ones form phage-defense systems that sense chopped-up host DNA.
plain_idea.train_on: The project considered: the supplementary table of MisB sensor-protein homologs drawn from 38,167 bacterial and archaeal genomes, embedded with a protein language model. The number of homolog rows is unknown - the paper never states it and the table could not be downloaded.
plain_idea.predict: Whether a candidate protein family actually aborts phage infection. The true answer comes from plaque assays (counting how many virus particles still form plaques when the system is present), done here for only about three or four systems against five phages.
plain_idea.why_worthwhile: Groups hunting new bacterial immune systems (Sorek, Nobrega, Laub labs) would use a reliable sensor-family predictor; but with roughly twenty measured outcomes in this paper, nothing can be trained or honestly evaluated.

more_or_better_data.why: DefensePredictor was trained and validated across 69 Escherichia coli strains with 42 experimentally confirmed systems; the companion language-model work scanned over 120 million proteins. This paper contributes about three or four tested systems.

confidence_score.why: Triplicate plaque assays exist for a handful of system-phage pairs, which is enough to estimate noise for those pairs but nowhere near enough to calibrate per-prediction confidence across protein families.

models_beatable.why: The competing models are 2025-2026, built on ESM-2 and genomic language models, and backed by prospective wet-lab validation (42 and 6 systems respectively) rather than a random split - the strongest kind of evaluation.

guaranteed_improvement.why: Fails almost every condition: this paper supplies no labelled training rows, no shared evaluation split, and its phenotype assays are not comparable to the defense-or-not labels those models were trained on.

ml_idea: The only machine-learning idea this paper supports is 'predict which bacterial protein families are anti-phage sensors from sequence', trained on its MisB homolog table. That task is already occupied by DefensePredictor and the ESM-2/genomic-language-model pair of Mordret et al., both with orders of magnitude more labels and prospective experimental validation. This paper's own measurements (about 3-4 systems x 5 phages, in triplicate) are a mechanism study, not a training set. The data would be worth revisiting only as a few extra positive examples inside a larger defense-system benchmark.

effort.compute_note: Size estimated from the single supplementary ZIP of four tables described in the preprint; nothing was downloaded or timed, because every download route was blocked (Science 403, bioRxiv 429).
effort.cheapest_killing_check: Count the rows in Supplementary Table S1 that carry a measured phage-protection outcome rather than just a homolog identifier. From the text the answer is roughly twenty, which kills it - and that is exactly what happened here.

verdict_reason: Part A fails on two counts. A1: nothing is deposited in any repository (no GEO, SRA, BioProject, Zenodo), the Science supplement is behind a subscription (HTTP 403) and the open preprint's single supplementary ZIP returned HTTP 429 to every programmatic attempt, so I opened no data file. A5: by the paper's own text the measured phenotype covers only about three or four cloned defense systems against five coliphages in triplicate, with the one large table (MisB homologs from 38,167 genomes) carrying no outcome column at all (A2). This is an excellent mechanism paper and a poor machine-learning substrate; the task it suggests is already held by DefensePredictor and by the ESM-2-based antiphage landscape models, both with far more labels.
